newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Belgian PM confident of meeting EMU deficit target.
newsitem.headline: Belgian PM confident of meeting EMU deficit target.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene expressed confidence on Tuesday that his country would cut its public sector deficit to below the EMU target of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year.
"In 1997 we will finish below three percent," he told an audience of Dutch businessmen.

Government figures published earlier this month showed that the Belgian deficit amounted to 3.4 of GDP percent in 1996 - down from 4.1 percent in 1995 but higher than the government's original 1996 target of 3.0 percent.

Dehaene said government policy was geared to ensuring that Belgium met the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) criteria so that it could take part in the planned launch of the European Union's single currency, the Euro, on January 1, 1999.
The government had been authorised to take swift remedial action, if needed, to make sure the country stayed on track for the single currency, he told reporters before making his speech.
It had already implemented supplementary measures in the area of health insurance, he said.
Dehaene said Belgium's EMU performance was among the best in Europe when it came to criteria such as inflation, interest rates and exchange rate stability.
Its 1996 deficit of 3.4 percent, he said, was even better than Germany's which he put at 3.9 percent.
Between 1993 and 1997 Belgium's public debt to GDP ratio would fall by 10 percentage points, showing good progress towards the EMU target of 60 percent, he said.
Belgian government figures published earlier this month showed public debt had fallen to 130.2 percent of GDP at the end of 1996 from 133.7 percent a year earlier.
